title: Make Recognition More Specific
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post makes the case that most leaders recognize good work too generally, wasting a chance to boost engagement and self-motivation. The author contrasts throwaway phrases such as good job with recognition that ties a specific contribution to a specific outcome, offering several before-and-after examples. Drawing on the widely cited finding that specific feedback is more actionable, the post extends the logic to praise: vivid, detailed recognition makes the underlying behaviors repeatable and shows everyone what quality looks like. The practical close is a simple instruction to describe exactly what the person did and why it affected the result, which leaves the recipient both valued and clear on what to do next time.
points: Generic praise like nice job motivates little, while praise that links a behavior to an outcome drives future performance.
Specific recognition does double duty: it makes the person feel valued and makes the behavior repeatable.
Vivid, detailed praise sets a visible standard of quality for the rest of the team.
The method is easy to apply: state exactly what the person did and why it mattered to the outcome.
quotes: Unfortunately, most leaders are too general in their acknowledgment and miss an opportunity to boost engagement and add jet fuel to self-motivation. Team members want to know when their work matters, and that their leader fully recognizes the contribution they have made.

Generic praise generally falls flat. “Good job” is a throwaway line that does little to motivate future performance. Better leaders go further. They link the distinct contributions of team members to specific outcomes.
Research consistently shows that feedback is more actionable when it is highly specific. The same is true with recognition. Specificity makes a huge difference.
When leaders are detailed in their recognition, team members feel more highly valued. The best leaders don’t just offer praise. They describe it in full color.

Being specific makes the behaviors underlying the recognition more repeatable. Better yet, leaders who connect the dots and make their descriptions of praise highly vivid and definitive validate what quality looks like for everyone.
The next time you call out great work, be specific. Describe exactly what the team member did and why it made an impact on the outcome.
